item.title: Fire devastates former Nazi guest house 'Eagle's Nest'
item.description: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Firefighters battled for hours to contain a blaze that engulfed the former Nazi guest house known as "The Eagle's Nest" in southern Germany, while police investigated the cause after detaining a man near the scene, authorities said on Saturday. Around 200 firefighters and emergency workers near Berchtesgaden in Bavaria were battling the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, caught fire on Friday, police said. Built in 1938 as a guest house for Nazi officials and their guests, the building sits in a spectacular Alpine setting above Berchtesgaden. Adolf Hitler used it occasionally, earning it the nickname "Hitler's Tea House". It is separate from his nearby summer residence, the Berghof. Bild newspaper quoted a police spokesperson as saying the building, preserved after World War Two as a historical monument linked to the Nazi era, had been so badly damaged that it "could probably not be saved". Police said earlier they had detained a man near the site but had not yet established the cause of the fire. "Whether the person is linked to the fire is currently the subject of a criminal investigation," Bavarian police said in a statement.

item.title: US accuses government contractor of leaking classified info to girlfriend's Substack
item.description: The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Trotta
item.content:encoded: The US Justice Department accused a government contractor on Friday of leaking national defense information to his girlfriend, the publisher of a Substack newsletter. The FBI arrested Ian Brinksman, 42, on Friday following a search of his Washington home, a Justice Department statement said. Prosecutors charged him with unlawfully transmitting national defense information. A federal public defender representing Brinksman declined to comment. “As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the statement. “That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably,” Eisenberg said. Brinksman held a top secret security clearance while working as an employee of a US government agency and later as a developer for systems integration for a private contractor working for the same agency, prosecutors said. According to the sworn affidavit of an FBI agent investigating the case, Brinksman repeatedly accessed classified intelligence reports and then communicated with the journalist. The affidavit also cites phone records, database access logs, badge-swipe records, emails and other evidence. The affidavit only identifies the journalist as "Individual 1," but it cites excerpts from articles she published. "A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 stated 'over the past year (Individual 1 has) published reporting based on classified (relevant U.S. government agency) assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about,'" the affidavit reads. That quote appears in a September 28 piece published on the Capital & Empire online newsletter authored by Aída Chávez. "Over the past year, I’ve published reporting based on classified CIA assessments that I believe the public deserves to know about," wrote Chávez, whose profile on the site notes that she worked for the Nation and other outlets before she launched the newsletter. Chávez did not respond to an email message seeking comment. Investigators allege that on at least five occasions in 2026, Individual 1 published Substack articles containing information that mirrored the classified reports, some at the top secret level. On some of those dates, Chávez published articles that cite classified reports, some of them attributed to the CIA. According to a LinkedIn profile bearing Brinksman's name, he worked for Deloitte as a manager and as a senior strategy security consultant after having worked as a US State Department foreign service officer on dates corresponding to those outlined in the Justice Department statement. The State Department declined to comment. Deloitte did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: US has for years asked Musk to alter Starlink service in Ukraine, Middle East, sources say
item.description: The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe.
item.dc:creator: Erin Banco, Joey Roulette
item.content:encoded: Well before the throttling this month of Ukraine's military access to Elon Musk's satellite communications system, the Biden and Trump administrations had several times asked SpaceX to turn its Starlink service on or off in various countries, according to six former senior US officials familiar with the matter. During the presidency of Joe Biden, the requests included switching off the service to prevent Iranian proxy militias in Yemen and Lebanon from using Starlink to communicate, and activating the service to provide internet access inside Iran and in Ukraine to support its military, said four of the former officials. Similarly, President Donald Trump's administration asked Musk, who is CEO of SpaceX, to make the service available in Iran following US-Israeli strikes in 2025 and 2026, in hopes it would bolster internet access and communications for anti-government protesters, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. All of the people spoke on condition of anonymity. The previous US requests about Starlink access are being reported here for the first time. The recent blowup over restrictions to Ukraine's use of SpaceX satellite services has raised questions about the ties between the US government and Musk, whose company owns systems vital to the US military and to US allies. The Biden-era and Trump requests to Musk show a close relationship in which US administrations rely to an unprecedented degree on a private-sector company to help implement foreign policy. The recent limits on Ukraine, despite being a US ally, have also rattled officials in Europe, some of whom argue that Europe must develop its own military satellite communications capabilities because no viable short-term alternative currently exists. STARSHIELD RESTRICTIONS HOBBLE UKRAINE MILITARY Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said last week that his country's access to Starshield, the military version of the Starlink system, had been intentionally limited, interfering with the performance of the country’s military drones. He also said the speeds were reduced for Starlink, which Ukraine uses for some military activities including defense against Russian missile attacks. Reuters has reported that [USN:L1N4610ZC TEXT:"the order to throttle Starshield"] came from inside the White House. The Trump administration has acknowledged the slowdown but has not said whether it gave the order. The White House, contacted for comment, referred Reuters to Trump's remarks on Friday, when he said he had not spoken with Musk about Starlink access issues for Ukraine and that "if there is a problem, I'll get it straightened out." Halyna Yusypiuk, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian embassy in Washington, said Ukraine's priority is "to have the service restored to normal speed as soon as possible, as the lives of our people depend on it." SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment, although Musk said in a social media post earlier this week: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately (by the president of the United States).” Democratic US Representative Jason Crow called on Friday for clarity about the recent changes to Ukraine's satellite service, saying there are risks to the US dependence on SpaceX. "Unelected billionaires and private corporations should not decide what is in the best interest of America's national security," Crow said. For Ukraine, the Starlink internet service has become the lifeblood of frontline communication between units, who say there is currently no rival to the capabilities of SpaceX's products. Starshield receivers, largely impervious to radio jamming, are used as onboard guidance systems and to provide links to a remote pilot for Ukrainian drones, including deep behind Russian lines inside Ukraine. MUSK'S INFLUENCE RAISES UNCERTAINTY Musk's role as the strong-willed CEO of a company with outsized influence over US national security has at times raised questions over who is making decisions about SpaceX's satellite services. The SpaceX CEO is "supposed to be a business executive, with government contracts, and he's essentially making huge foreign policy decisions," said Armand Musey, president of Summit Ridge Group, a satellite industry consultancy. "He's sufficiently ambiguous of a person that you don't know if his decisions are sort of his personal quirks, or it's because there's an influence elsewhere that's impacting him," Musey said. In previous years, Musk has moved to limit Ukraine’s access to Starlink. In 2022, according to Reuters reporting , Musk ordered SpaceX personnel to cut Starlink coverage in areas Ukraine was trying to retake, a move that surprised White House officials. Musk has said publicly that he refused a 2022 Ukrainian request to activate his satellite network in Crimea's port city of Sevastopol to aid an attack on Russia's fleet there, saying he feared complicity in a major act of war. The Biden administration at times relied on Musk to help implement policy, five of the former officials said. Biden officials coordinated with SpaceX to thwart US adversaries by cutting the service, and to help allies by expanding Starlink’s availability, they said. They added that discussions between the government and SpaceX, which usually included Pentagon and White House officials, often focused on preventing groups such as the Iranian-linked Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon from using Starlink terminals. Biden officials several times shared intelligence with SpaceX that indicated that the Houthis and Hezbollah were using diverted Starlink terminals — hardware that made its way to the militants through intermediaries. In October 2023, during fighting between Israel and Hezbollah militants in southern Lebanon, intelligence officials told the White House that individuals linked to Hezbollah could have gained access to Starlink terminals. Officials had similar concerns about the Houthis in Yemen in 2024 during a US air campaign against the Iran-linked group, five of the officials said. In both cases, the administration contacted SpaceX and asked it to identify the terminals and shut them off. At least some of the terminals were deactivated, said two of the officials. In a 2024 submission to the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, SpaceX said it works closely with US government agencies to secure export authorizations where required and to safeguard technology in support of US national security objectives and foreign policy goals. Soon after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Biden officials pushed SpaceX to expand Starlink use for the Ukrainian military, said two of the former officials. In a separate instance, the Biden administration asked SpaceX to turn on Starlink in Iran during a protest movement launched in September 2022 after the death of Mahsa Amini, an Iranian arrested for not wearing her hijab properly, according to one of the former officials. Starlink terminals were moved into the country with the help of the administration, said the official, who declined to say how many were transferred. The Trump administration took a similar step earlier this year and discussed with Musk and SpaceX getting Starlink terminals into Iran and activated following US-Israeli strikes in the country in June 2025 and again in February 2026, a former senior Trump official and a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Neither the Trump administration nor SpaceX has publicly confirmed that those terminals were turned on. The Wall Street Journal reported in February that the US government had sent thousands of Starlink terminals into Iran. Iran's delegation to the UN did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Fear factory
item.description: How filmmakers turn psychological triggers, practical effects and modest budgets into some of Hollywood's most profitable movies
item.dc:creator: Tiana McGee, Anurag Rao, Travis Hartman
item.content:encoded: Before the film, a cinema fills with rows of seats. Choose a rating, put on headphones, and watch a red door with a peephole loom closer. The camera pushes through the peephole into a dark hallway, where something is waiting. Reduce motion R **May contain jump scares PG Click headphones to turn sound on Before every horror film comes a warning. Not about what’s on the screen; about what it might do to you. Choose your experience wisely. Horror is something you experience, not just watch. You sit back, the lights dim, and you plunge into darkness. A feeling of unease starts to settle on you, but you can’t look away. Instead, Horror invites you to look closer. Something looks off. Everything is too quiet. Your body tenses. Your toes curl. You feel like the smallest thing in the room. Your heart is pounding in your chest and then – Just a glimpse and then it’s gone. But you know it’s still there. A creature. An unknown danger. A silent promise waiting to be kept. Fear Factory How filmmakers turn psychological triggers, practical effects and modest budgets into some of Hollywood's most profitable movies By Tiana McGee , Anurag Rao and Travis Hartman Published October 23, 2026 Fear Factory By Tiana McGee , Anurag Rao and Travis Hartman Published Oct. 23, 2026 06:00 AM EDT Horror movies have seen a dramatic rise in both critical acclaim and financial success. The genre has long been one of the safer box-office bets for studios wringing big returns out of modest budgets. Now, in an industry still recovering from the pandemic, that reliability has become a beacon. Because of this dependability, Michelle Martinez, a senior instructor at Arizona State University’s Film and Media Studies program, sees horror as Hollywood’s lifeline. “That’s how we persist,” she said. “Horror film has always been a ‘yes and’ sport. It’s always been low-budget. Nobody took it seriously until now, really.” We're gonna need a bigger box office Horror films are taking up a larger chunk of the domestic box office. In recent years, a single film has dominated each year’s share. This year’s summer blockbuster Obsession made up almost 29% of horror’s overall box office as of July. 5%10%15%20%0201220132014201520162017201820192020202120222023202420252026 Share of total box office The year's #1 horror film All other horror films A gash is cut across the top of the chart and blood falls out of it into fifteen pools, one per year from 2012 to 2026. Pool depth is horror’s share of total domestic box office, rising from 5.9% in 2012 to 18.2% in 2026, on an axis reading 50% at the cut down to zero at the floor. The bright blood at the foot of each pool is that year’s #1 horror film. Note: Data as of July; box office numbers are for the U.S. & Canada Source: Rentrak Horror isn’t just succeeding at the box office; critics are taking notice as well. Sinners , directed by Ryan Coogler, set in Jim Crow-era Mississippi Delta in 1932, received a record 16 Oscar nominations and earned Michael B. Jordan his first Oscar for Best Actor, marking a distinct return for the genre as a critic darling. In the 1970s and 80s, the slasher subgenre dominated the scene after the success of Halloween in 1978. The rise of VHS helped horror movies with limited releases find much-needed permanent homes on video store shelves, giving audiences greater access and opening the door for films to become cult classics. At the 64th Academy Awards in 1992, The Silence of the Lambs became the first and currently only horror film to win Best Picture. However, the 2000s marked a lull for the genre until 2017, when Jordan Peele’s Get Out seemed to announce a shift. All eyes on horror Horror films began to gain critical acclaim in the 1970s with The Exorcist . However, horror film award counts dropped off after 2000, until Get Out sparked a resurgence that continues today. Source: OMDb (Metacritic aggregate), matched against IMDb Horror-tagged titles. So, what does it mean to make art designed to scare people? Nine ways the camera works on you Different camera techniques have long been one of the most effective tools for unsettling audiences. Here are nine common examples: Dolly zoom Dutch angle Bird's eye view Mirrors Close-ups Off-center subjects Camera behind something POV Shaky cam The dolly zoom pulls you into the character’s mindset during tense moments Creative camera placement adds tension and suspense A bird’s eye view offers distance, so you watch the drama unfold A Dutch angle tilts the shot to signal unease POV shots immerse you in the character’s perspective All movies are built on balancing moments of tension with moments of release or relaxation for viewers. In horror movies, this becomes especially important. Moments of peace, even mundane ones, can lure the audience into a false sense of security. A lull can trick you into letting your guard down before the next high-tension moment/scare. With jump scares, there are often moments of silence or softness before the scare. After these moments, a sudden, sharp musical chord or loud sound effect known as the sting typically occurs at the same moment the threat/danger appears. “It might open with some gore just to set the tone or have a little early pre-scare just to prime you,” Martinez said. “So that you’re ready for the bigger build.” Prepare for a SCARE! Each mark below represents a jumpscare. Over the film’s two-hour runtime, it has 11 scares, but they don’t arrive on a schedule. The first arrives 11 minutes in, three cluster in a four-minute burst around the 30-minute mark, the longest calm runs 25 minutes through the second hour, and the final two land 18 seconds apart with 10 minutes of film still to go. Note: whenjumpscare.com rates none of these 11 as major; that is a judgment about how each moment is staged, not a verdict on how frightening the film is. Correlation only — dense jumpscares are also the house style of low-budget and late-franchise horror, which critics mark down for many reasons at once. The score, and other sounds that occur outside the world of the story, can be used to manipulate you into feeling tense in moments where you may not even notice it consciously. Sounds that do exist in the world of the film, whispers or floorboards creaking, suggest that something is not as it should be. Lighting, too, is a pivotal choice for making horror work. Shadows and darkness keep things from the audience, letting them imagine the worst. Horror often uses what’s just out of reach to scare and disturb you. Click to turn out the lights The genre works well as a powerful lens for telling larger stories. Horror, like many other art forms, can reflect societal issues, offering a cathartic way to process hardship and trauma across different communities. By transforming real experiences into frightening yet safe scenarios, horror lets us confront hard topics in a controlled environment. Carrie , a movie based on Stephen King’s novel about a bullied high school girl raised by a fanatically religious and abusive mother, is a front-of-mind example for Martinez. The 1974 novel and the Brian De Palma film are often connected to the landmark abortion rights ruling of Roe v. Wade a year earlier, as both express themes of bodily autonomy and the consequences of “the repressing of female power.” Get Out serves as a social commentary on race and Black exploitation. Released in 2017, the film reflects the evolving discussions around race relations and systemic racism at the time. And films like the summer blockbuster Obsession return to questions of autonomy and critique modern dating culture, turning the “Nice Guy” trope on its head. Horror can also give the audience a safe space to work through emotion. Martinez finds that in her classes, it comes up a lot. “If you’re somebody that’s grieving and you go watch a horror film, it helps you push out that wave of grief,” She said. “When you have art that makes you feel […] It helps you reset. And I think for a lot of people, that’s why they really like it. With horror movies making a comeback in a big way, it’s easy to get swept up in the numbers and why they work, but for Martinez, it’s a bit simpler than that. Horror, she says, is a way to break out of the monotony of daily drudgery. “That’s what musicals do. That’s what horror does. It pinches you awake.” Edited by Julia Wolfe, Nick Zieminski

item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Environ 1.200 Palestiniens déplacés à Hébron par une opération militaire israélienne JÉRUSALEM, 24 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée israélienne a contraint environ 1.200 Palestiniens à quitter leurs foyers à Hébron, en Cisjordanie occupée, a déclaré samedi un responsable palestinien, au lendemain d'une attaque qui a coûté la vie à deux soldats israéliens. Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande. Le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un en visite en Chine Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen. L'Ukraine dit que Starlink refonctionne normalement Le système de communication par satellites Starlink et sa version militaire Starshield fonctionnent à nouveau à des vitesses supérieures à 400 km/h, a déclaré samedi le ministre ukrainien de la Défense. La Russie et l'Ukraine acceptent un cessez-le-feu à Oleshky La Russie et l'Ukraine ont accepté de respecter un cessez-le-feu dans la ville ukrainienne d'Oleshky, occupée par la Russie, afin de permettre l'évacuation des civils pris au piège des combats, a annoncé vendredi la Maison blanche. L'Autriche expulse quatre diplomates russes, Moscou promet de répliquer Le ministère autrichien des Affaires étrangères a annoncé vendredi l'expulsion de quatre diplomates russes basés à Vienne en raison "d'activités incompatibles avec leur statut diplomatique", expression généralement employée pour des faits d'espionnage. La Corée du Sud propose à nouveau de discuter avec la Corée du Nord de la frontière terrestre Le ministère sud-coréen de la Défense a de nouveau proposé vendredi la tenue de pourparlers militaires avec la Corée du Nord, afin de s'accorder sur le tracé exact de la frontière terrestre entre les deux Corées et de réduire le risque d'affrontements accidentels. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde menacées par les feux de forêt Les plus anciennes peintures rupestres du monde, situées sur l'île indonésienne de Sulawesi, sont menacées par la chaleur et la fumée générées par les pires feux de forêt que le pays ait connus depuis plus d'une décennie, ont déclaré des chercheurs. Arabie saoudite: Nouveau report de forums internationaux à 2027 Deux nouveaux forums internationaux prévus en cette fin d'année en Arabie saoudite ont été reportés à 2027 en raison des attaques que lancent les Houthis, rebelles yéménites proches de l'Iran, sur le royaume, a déclaré vendredi l'Autorité générale des statistiques du pays.
